newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria sanctions funds for misleading adverts.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria sanctions funds for misleading adverts.

text.p: Bulgaria' Securities and Stock Exchanges Commission (SSEC) has fined eight privatisation funds for using misleading information in their advertising campaigns aimed at attracting more subscribers to their funds.
"The range of offences is very wide and we will continue our checks for irregularites in other funds," SSEC chairman Kristian Tanoushev told a news conference on Friday.
SSEC licensed 96 privatisation funds this year. They are empowered to collect vouchers from the population and participate in mass privatisation tenders due to begin in October.
Under Bulgaria's mass privatisation programme launched last year stakes in some 1,060 state enterprises will be offered for mass sell-offs.
"The most ludicrous is the campaign of the Nadejda (Hope) privatisation fund, which promised $50 to the first 50,000 shareholders," said Tanoushev.
The fund failed to provide proof that it had set aside $250,000 for such payments and SSEC stopped the misleading advertisement, said Tanoushev.

The Nadejda fund also said that an unnamed Swiss bank was "supporting the fund". SSCE checks showed that the fund only had a settlement account in a Swiss bank without any other guarantees and asked the fund to delete this information from its ads.

Other funds like Orel Invest also used names of foreign banks and foreign airlines as sponcors to boost their image. But SSEC checks showed that the support form Austrian Airlines in this case was provided only in the form of five free plane tickets.

When asked which funds were more reliable, Tanoushev said that the bigger funds with subscribed capital exceeding two billion levs had more chances to remain afloat. Of the 96 registered, some 10 privatisation funds meet that condition.

Pyramid investment schemes, which proved popular in several post-communist countries attracted more than 30,000 Bulgarians in the past few years. The depositors lost all their savings when $25 million sank into the get-rich-quick schemes, after their owners fled with the money. -- Elisaveta Konstantinova, Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
